beginnings: The keeper has brought supper for two. A slip in the empty bowl has the same mark as the docket.
Yesterday a family paid a fee on the strength of this signature. The keeper recognises their own thumb in the ink.
A child can read just one word on the case. Today somebody has pasted a price over it.
Two neighbours remember the tune. They stop at the same bar and each waits for the other to finish it.
The joiner knows which corner catches on a sleeve. Someone has sanded it smooth overnight.
There is a bare patch on the shelf. Under the dust lies a wet ring the size of a cup.
The midday light passes through the case. An extra notch appears on the paper lying under it.
A tiny silver trophy rattles in the drawer. One witness laughs. The keeper asks to see the engraving.
Floodwater left a dark line on the porter’s coat. The parcel in their hands has dry paper feet.
A girl draws the room for the sixth time. Each drawing includes the spot where she stood.
The apprentice drops the key when the visitor takes out a gold pencil. The visitor stoops to pick it up.
A parcel comes wrapped in a scarf. The keeper turns a darned corner under before you can read the initials.
Two adults tip the board towards each other. A child slips under it and reads the underside aloud.
Ash catches in three cracks in the case. The cracks cross in a different order on the rubbing.
An older neighbour asks to hear the notice read out again. This time they ask where the reader took a breath.
The goat is chewing the corner of a receipt. The receipt clerk is offering it their lunch in exchange.
At dawn the queue moves one seat at a time. Everyone who gets up leaves their chair facing a different way.
The keeper calls for a key without taking a hand off the case. A key on their own belt swings into sight.
An apprentice has chalked the date above the school door. Today the digits run in the opposite direction.
Someone put a maker’s apron in the display case. It still has the night porter’s house key in the pocket.
The invitation calls it an unveiling. At the back a woman is quietly taking her name off the guest list.
A runner knows the shortcut by its old name. The new sign sends them back to the same lamp.
The last visitor to leave was carrying flowers. This morning the paper stems are pointing at the latch.
A brass bird calls out a price. By noon the stalls are copying the bird, including its little hiccup.
leads: Someone moved the docket in the night. Follow the black dust off the string.
The dust ends at a child's eye level. The night porter lowered the copy so their son could read it before school.
A weight has vanished between the first and second lists. Look at what each clerk carried.
One clerk kept the case on the pan. The other weighed the empty travelling sling separately.
All six copies break off at the very same letter. Hold their edges to the light.
Six different hands copied a sheet with a hole in it. The agreement goes back to one damaged witness.
Two names fit the space where one has been rubbed out. Try the soft pencil on the back.
The second name was the person who mended the stand. Both people had once been listed under the word maker.
The old road is missing from the earliest chart. Listen for the part the ferryman hums.
The dock used to move. The line in the tune measures time under oar, and the landing has shifted since.
A date on the duplicate is a year younger. Match it with the little rent receipt.
The stall kept its accounts from first frost. The keeper at the gate started again in spring.
The stamp is real. Where did the coin come from?
Three stallholders pooled their pennies for one seal. Each thought the other two had tried the instrument.
A portrait in the office shows a crate that has not arrived. Look closely at its shadow.
The painter borrowed the empty packing stand. The porter added the crate in chalk for the next shift.
Someone at the festival stopped speaking halfway through a name. Find the second listener.
The singer had promised a family a hearing before using their name in public. The second listener took the rest at home.
There is a crescent beneath every copy on the rack. Turn the rack a quarter turn.
The crescent moves with the bent clasp. It records the rack that held the slips.
The clerk with the coldest hands remembers a warm room. Test the two seats.
The hot pipe runs under one seat. The keeper at the far window had an equally good reason to remember frost.
Anonymous letters arrive in different hands. All of them have the same fold.
A porter lends out one folding board. Several people signed their own letters after the folds had hidden the signatures.
The river song has two endings. Count where the homeward crew dips its oars.
One ending guides a loaded boat, the other an empty one. The extra rest gives the heavier boat time to turn.
The case has a second set of screw holes. The keeper has the old lid in their lap.
A smaller apprentice made the first lid open at arm’s reach. Their teacher changed the height for a taller visitor.
A crate went missing while people stood watching it. Compare the porter’s two tickets.
The ticket marked missing belonged to the outward journey. It reached the desk a tide after the return ticket.
Someone took a knife to the page. Look for the letters on the reverse.
The letters run over the torn edge onto a smaller sheet. The witness kept a promise by giving the missing strip to its addressee.
At noon two shadows point in opposite directions. Cover the little window in the case.
One shadow disappears under your palm. The glass was returning light from the other side of the room.
The flowers are renewed even when the room is locked. Ask the person who waters the sill.
The flowers are made of paper. Every morning a different neighbour turns one petal towards the glass.
The sealed packet rattles. The day keeper has always called it empty.
A tiny bell was left inside to tell a listener when the packet moved. The day keeper has never carried it.
The key fits only halfway home. Compare the two notches with a returning traveller.
The other notch fits the next town’s lock. The two keepers used to pass the key downriver together.
The sign promises silence. Something answers behind it when a visitor moves.
A board below the seat taps the next wall. Two visitors on opposite sides heard each other stand.
Two boxes carry the same number. Check who wrote the fraction after it.
The stores clerk counted a pair as one loan. The family collecting one half had written a fraction in charcoal.
The richest bid for a parcel was withdrawn. Try turning the bid slip over.
The bidder had asked for an evening loan. Only the first side appeared in the public list.
One corner of a drawing is rubbed smooth. Watch which hand lifts it first.
A visitor who reads by touch found the joint years before the keepers noticed the seam in their drawing.
keeps: The person on the late shift can inspect the change before putting their name to it.
A borrower folds the first account into their sleeve and volunteers to bring it back tomorrow.
The night runner comes back for the small print. Someone has put a chair by the lamp for them.
The person who first raised the alarm leaves their name on the correction. Their friend leaves theirs beside it.
A child turns the slip over and explains the blank to the adult who brought them.
The porter makes a second hook. Tomorrow there will be room for a different reading.
